Turner explicitly gives Shina astóm judgement under *āsthāman meeting place and marks the Burushaski equivalent as borrowed from Shina. Degener’s Burushaski comparison therefore does not require reversing the donor direction.
Turner records Shina gaṭóĭki earn and gaṭṇi income under *ghaṭyate. Degener’s win sense agrees with acquisition/procurement, though the semantic extension should be reviewed.

Degener explicitly calls yar- cause to go the causative of yai-. The base’s historical derivation remains tentative in the preceding proposal; this immediate morphological link is explicit.

Turner’s addendum 14396 explicitly suggests Shina kunāli stick/kunālo walking-stick as a possible extension of kunta. Degener notes a Burushaski counterpart; keep the extension and contact history tentative.
Turner explicitly gives Gilgit boĭki become under bhavati; bhūta instead accounts for past bulu. Both source references describe parts of the paradigm, so this stem is assigned to bhavati.

Turner explicitly records Shina čhubóĭki place under chupati, with influence from kṣubhyati. Preserve that mixed formation rather than claiming unconditioned retention of b.

Turner’s addendum 14404 explicitly reanalyses kuyōč as a derivative of Shina kui with suffix -ōč(h), rather than requiring direct inheritance of reconstructed *kūpatya. The suffix’s deeper origin remains uncertain.

Turner explicitly places Shina ṣakāe pair of scales under tarka, through *tarkaḍa. Degener’s 5716 reference points to the related looking verb; the noun belongs under 5714.
Turner explicitly compares Shina kači near with a possible locative kakṣyē, alongside Torwali kač. Retain Turner’s question mark: the locative origin is a hypothesis.

Turner assigns Shina lamuṭo/lamōṭu tail to subsection 3 *lāṅguṭṭa, with influence from lamba long. The proposed family preserves this mixed formation rather than treating m as an unexplained regular outcome.

Turner’s later addendum 14792 explicitly gives Shina bam mare, plural bāme, from *vaḍam(b)ā through *bayam, and marks Burushaski as borrowed from Shina. This supplies the missing Shina evidence in the main vaḍabā entry; retain the intermediate reconstruction.

Degener’s primary glossary explicitly analyzes sam well as probably from sāma, referring to Turner 13346 and attributing the suggestion to Buddruss. The full Turner entry groups sāmaka even/level and sāma likeness/sameness; it does not itself cite Shina. This is therefore a tentative semantic development from even/equal to well/good, supported by Degener’s qualified proposal rather than a direct Turner attestation. The head record represents that grouped entry; no unexplained -ka reflex is asserted. The Backstrom/Schmidt good attestations and the well attestation share sam, but their grammatical gloss differences are preserved.

Degener explicitly analyzes ṣa-māzo six-month with Turner 12803 six and 10104 month. The proposal represents the native Shina numeral and month noun as ordered components. The final adjectival vowel remains part of the recorded compound, rather than being treated as a separate lexical root.

Degener explicitly assigns ṣéewo blind to CDIAL 12717, whose first branch lists Shina ṣevo beside Phalura ṣīṛu and Kalasha ṣēṛä. Turner discusses competing *śīrta/*śriḍa and expressive rhyme-family histories, so *śrēḍa is a dictionary-family placement, not an established unique reconstruction or a claim that every loss of v/w has been independently demonstrated.

Degener p. 305 táalo Gaumendach independently supplies the precise roof-of-mouth sense; her note compares Berger’s tonsil sense and Burushaski dáalumuċ tonsillitis without explicitly establishing a Burushaski donor.

This assigns the cited Shina family while retaining the unresolved aspiration and remote reconstruction.

Degener p. 291 explicitly derives pāo-pēsā money from Urdu pāo quarter-anna and paisā coin/money; these are paired money terms, not a claim that the expression means a quarter of a paisa. The ordered Hindi-Urdu donor nodes distinguish pāu quarter from foot, and Platts independently confirms paisā as a quarter-anna coin and money, supporting the immediate donor sense despite Shina ē versus Urdu ai.

Degener p. 311 puts ũcij- become a spring immediately after ũc spring of water and supplies the future plural ũciijen. This is a same-language inchoative formation from the noun, whose ancestry CDIAL 1869 útsa explicitly supports with Gilgit nasalized ũc; it is not a direct inherited reflex of the Sanskrit noun.

Degener p. 268 lists haliẓ- turn yellow (of the complexion), future haliẓéi, directly beside halíẓo yellow. A same-language deadjectival analysis is inferred from the identical stem and change-of-state meaning; CDIAL 13990 supports the adjective’s ancestry but does not itself list this verb.

Degener p. 251 explicitly identifies beyarij- be made to sit as the passive of the causative of bēi- sit. The proposed same-language derivation records both operations, without inventing an unattested intermediate causative node or treating it as a direct reflex of Sanskrit upavēśayati; Turner’s uncertainty about the deeper sitting family remains with the base.

Degener p. 276 places kolij- become crooked, warp; remain silent, without answer beside kōlo crooked. The inchoative -ij formation from that adjective is a morphological inference, with the source’s additional silence sense retained; CDIAL 3533 supports the adjective rather than directly attesting the verb.

Degener p. 279 lists khacyār badness, misfortune beside kháco bad and its feminine kháči; Turner’s addendum 14343 also records Shina khacár ingratitude in this expressive-aspiration family. Propose an abstract formation from the same-source adjective, retaining the y and the semantic extension rather than equating the whole noun with an inherited adjective.

Degener p. 302 places šiār goodness, prosperity alongside ši- be good, thrive, be prosperous; the matching stem and meanings support an abstract derivation, comparable structurally with khacyār badness and ragoṭyār illness. This is a same-language morphological inference, not a direct assignment of the abstract noun to *śubhyati.

Degener p. 302 explicitly derives šidalar- let cool down from šidálo cold and attests the absolutive šidalare. Link the verb to that same-source Shina adjective as a causative formation; Turner’s unexplained d in the wider śītala family concerns the base’s prehistory, not this explicitly identified local relationship.

Degener explicitly glosses phacī little tail and identifies it as formed from phacō tail, marking the diminutive noun feminine against the masculine base. Use a same-language derived link; CDIAL 8249 supports the base’s extended tail family, without making the diminutive a separate inherited reflex.

Degener explicitly calls buchēro little calf a variant of bacharō and also records its use as a personal name. CDIAL 11241 vatsatara gives Shina bachar/basero and Bshk. bachēr, supporting the r-bearing calf family; retain the changed vowel pattern and diminutive sense rather than collapsing it into the distinct bachō calf entry under vatsa.

The latter replaces the adjectival -o with the Shina abstract formation -yār, also represented in the reviewed adjective/abstract pairs; link the local size noun to its Shina adjective rather than directly to the remote vaḍra head.

Degener explicitly defines adāpi as a girl who was not given a dāp dowry. This supports the local negative formation a-dāp-i, retaining the feminine ending and connecting it to the independently recorded marriage-payment noun; Turner 6279 corroborates Shina dāp but is not the immediate parent of this adjective.
